title: 돌발 주제 모음
intro: 돌발 주제는 설문에서 선택하지 않아도 무작위로 나오는 주제로, 날씨·교통·재활용·전화기·인터넷·명절·가구·은행 등이 단골입니다. 모든 돌발 주제를 따로 준비하는 건 불가능하므로, 시간을 버는 문장과 '과거 vs 현재', '나의 하루', '기억에 남는 일' 같은 만능 패턴을 어떤 주제에나 끼워 넣는 것이 전략입니다. 내용의 정확성보다 멈추지 않고 말하는 유창성이 훨씬 중요합니다.
strategy: 질문을 받으면 'That's an interesting question. Let me think for a second.' 으로 3초를 벌고, 그 사이 답변 구조(묘사/일과/경험/비교)를 정합니다.
모르는 주제라도 'These days, more and more people ~ / Back in the day, ~' 패턴으로 과거·현재 비교를 만들면 어떤 주제든 1분을 채울 수 있습니다.
경험 질문은 무조건 과거시제 + 시간 순서(언제 → 무슨 일 → 내 행동 → 결과 → 느낌)로, 내용은 평범해도 괜찮습니다.

expressions.en: That's an interesting question. Let me think for a second.
I'm not an expert, but I'd say it depends on the person.
These days, more and more people use their phones for everything.
expressions.ko: 요즘은 점점 더 많은 사람이 모든 걸 휴대폰으로 해요.

expressions.en: Back in the day, we didn't have smartphones, so life was simpler.
expressions.ko: 예전에는 스마트폰이 없어서 삶이 더 단순했어요.

expressions.en: In Korea, we have four distinct seasons.
I usually take the subway because it's fast and cheap.
expressions.ko: 저는 보통 지하철을 타요, 빠르고 싸니까요.

expressions.en: In Korea, we have to separate our trash into paper, plastic, glass, and food waste.
expressions.note: 재활용 주제: separate A into B

expressions.en: I can't imagine living without my phone.
expressions.ko: 휴대폰 없는 삶은 상상이 안 돼요.

expressions.en: Speaking of holidays, I remember one Chuseok when the whole family got stuck in traffic.
expressions.ko: 명절 얘기가 나와서 말인데, 온 가족이 교통 체증에 갇혔던 추석이 기억나요.

expressions.en: It's not something I think about every day, but now that you mention it, I do have a story.
expressions.ko: 매일 생각하는 건 아닌데, 말씀하시니까 생각나는 이야기가 하나 있어요.
expressions.note: now that you mention it = 말씀하시니까

expressions.en: Compared to ten years ago, things are a lot more convenient now.
The good thing is that it's convenient, but the downside is that it can be addictive.
expressions.ko: 좋은 점은 편리하다는 거고, 안 좋은 점은 중독될 수 있다는 거예요.

expressions.en: If I had to pick one, I'd go with the subway over the bus.
expressions.ko: 하나만 골라야 한다면 버스보다 지하철을 택할 거예요.

expressions.en: To be honest, it's a bit of a hassle, but it's become second nature to me.
expressions.ko: 솔직히 좀 번거롭긴 한데, 이제는 몸에 완전히 배었어요.

expressions.en: Looking back, I can't believe how much things have changed in such a short time.
expressions.ko: 돌아보면 이렇게 짧은 시간에 이렇게 많이 바뀌었다는 게 믿기지 않아요.

questions.en: Tell me about the weather in your country. What are the seasons like, and which season do you like the most?
questions.ko: 당신 나라의 날씨에 대해 말해 주세요. 계절은 어떤가요? 어느 계절을 가장 좋아하나요?
tips: 사계절 순서대로 한 문장씩 → 가장 좋아하는 계절 + 이유
'In Korea, we have four distinct seasons' 로 시작하면 구조가 잡혀요

answers.IM3: In Korea, we have four distinct seasons. Spring is warm, and there are cherry blossoms everywhere. Summer is very hot and humid, and it rains a lot in July. Fall is cool and sunny, and the leaves turn red and yellow. Winter is cold and dry, and it sometimes snows. My favorite season is fall because the weather is perfect for walking. Also, the sky is very clear and blue. I don't like summer because it's too hot.
answers.IH: Well, Korea has four distinct seasons, and each one feels really different. Spring, from March to May, is mild and beautiful, with cherry blossoms all over the city. The problem is the fine dust, which can be pretty bad in spring. Summer is hot and humid, and we have a rainy season in July when it rains almost every day. In August, it can go up to 35 degrees, so I basically live with the air conditioner on. Fall is my favorite, hands down. The weather is cool and dry, the sky is clear, and the leaves turn red and gold. It's perfect for walking along the river after work. Winter is cold and dry, and it goes down to minus 10 sometimes. It snows a few times a year, which is pretty but makes the commute a hassle. To be honest, I feel like summer and winter are getting longer, and spring and fall are getting shorter. Still, I love that we get to experience all four.
answers.AL: Korea is known for having four distinct seasons, and honestly, they're distinct enough that it almost feels like living in four different countries. Spring rolls in around March. It's mild and gorgeous, with cherry blossoms lining the streets, but it's also fine dust season, so there are days when you can barely see the buildings across the river. Summer is a whole different beast. It's hot, humid, and sticky, and the rainy season in July means carrying an umbrella every day for about three weeks. By August, we're hitting 35 degrees, and I basically live in front of the air conditioner. Fall is my favorite by a mile. The humidity drops off, the sky turns this incredible deep blue, and the leaves go red and gold along the river near my apartment. It's the one time of year when I actually look forward to my walk to the subway. Then winter comes in hard and dry, with temperatures dipping to minus 10 or below. Snow is beautiful for about a day, until it turns into slush on the sidewalks. What I've noticed lately is that the in-between seasons seem to be getting shorter, which is a shame. Still, I wouldn't trade the variety for anything.

questions.en: How do you usually get around in your city? Tell me about the public transportation you use and what a typical trip is like.
questions.ko: 도시에서 보통 어떻게 이동하나요? 이용하는 대중교통과 일반적인 이동 과정에 대해 말해 주세요.
tips: 주로 쓰는 수단 → 출퇴근 과정(시간·환승) → 다른 수단 언급 → 장단점
'It takes me about 20 minutes', 'tap my card', 'rush hour' 활용

answers.IM3: I usually take the subway to get around Seoul. I live near a subway station, so it's very convenient. It takes me about 20 minutes to get to work. I use a transportation card, and I just tap it at the gate. The subway is fast and cheap, but it's very crowded in the morning. Sometimes I take the bus when I go shopping. On weekends, I like to walk if the place is close. I don't have a car because parking is difficult in Seoul.
answers.IH: Well, I get around almost entirely by public transportation. My apartment is a five-minute walk from a subway station, so the subway is my main way to travel. On weekdays, I leave home around 8:30, walk to the station, and take Line 2 for about 20 minutes to get to my office. I use a transportation card, so I just tap in and tap out, and the fare is only about 1,500 won. The subway is fast and reliable, but during rush hour it gets so crowded that I can barely move. On weekends, I sometimes take the bus instead because I can look out the window. Late at night, I'll take a taxi, which I call with an app. I don't own a car because parking in Seoul is a nightmare, and honestly, the subway is faster anyway. Compared to when I was a student, I think the system has gotten even better. The trains come every two or three minutes, and the app tells me exactly when the next one is coming.
answers.AL: I rely on public transportation for pretty much everything, which is easy to do in Seoul. My apartment is about a five-minute walk from a Line 2 station, so on weekdays, I'm out the door around 8:30, tap my card at the gate, and I'm at the office roughly 20 minutes later. The trains run every two or three minutes during rush hour, so I never really check the schedule. The downside, of course, is the crowd. Between 8 and 9 in the morning, it gets so packed that you're basically standing shoulder to shoulder, and I've learned to just put in my earbuds and zone out. On weekends, I tend to switch to the bus if I'm not in a hurry, mainly because I like looking out the window and it drops me closer to wherever I'm going. Late at night, I'll call a taxi through an app, which usually shows up within a few minutes. I've never owned a car, and I don't really plan to. Parking in Seoul is a nightmare, and honestly, the subway would beat me there anyway. Looking back at when I was a student, the system has only gotten better. Everything is on one card, transfers are free, and the app tells me down to the minute when my train is arriving.

questions.en: Tell me about recycling in your country. How does it work, and what do you do at home to recycle?
questions.ko: 당신 나라의 재활용에 대해 말해 주세요. 어떻게 이루어지고, 집에서는 재활용을 위해 무엇을 하나요?
tips: 한국의 제도(분리수거·종량제 봉투·음식물 쓰레기) → 우리 아파트 방식 → 내가 하는 일 → 느낌

answers.IM3: Recycling is very important in Korea. We have to separate our trash into paper, plastic, glass, cans, and food waste. We also have to buy special bags for regular trash. In my apartment, there is a recycling area on the first floor. I take my recycling there every Sunday evening. Before that, I wash the plastic bottles and remove the labels. Food waste goes in a separate bin. It's a little annoying, but I think it's good for the environment.
answers.IH: Recycling in Korea is pretty strict compared to a lot of countries. We have to separate our trash into paper, plastic, glass, cans, and food waste, and regular trash has to go in special designated bags that we buy at the convenience store. Food waste is separate, too, and in my apartment building, we weigh it with a card and pay by the kilogram. There's a recycling area on the first floor of my building, and it's only open on certain days. So every Sunday evening, I carry everything down in the elevator. Before that, I rinse out the plastic bottles, peel off the labels, and flatten the cardboard boxes. To be honest, it was a hassle when I first moved in, and I got it wrong a few times. Now it's just part of my routine. I've also started using a reusable cup at cafes to cut down on plastic. It's a lot of small steps, but I think Koreans are pretty good at it overall.
answers.AL: Recycling in Korea is taken pretty seriously, and to be honest, it's a bit of a system. Everything gets separated: paper, plastic, glass, cans, and food waste all go in different places, and regular trash has to go in designated bags that you buy at the convenience store. If you put the wrong thing in the wrong bag, you can actually get fined. Food waste is its own category. In my building, there's a bin that weighs it when you tap your card, and you pay by the kilogram, which honestly makes me think twice before letting leftovers go bad. The recycling area is on the first floor, and it's only open on certain days, so every Sunday evening, I make my trip down in the elevator with two or three bags. Before that, I rinse out the bottles, peel the labels off, and break down the cardboard boxes. When I first moved in, I found the whole thing a hassle, and I got a couple of warnings from the building manager for mixing things up. But it's become second nature at this point. I've also started carrying a reusable cup to cafes to cut down on plastic. It's a lot of little steps, but when you see how much a single building sorts in a week, it feels worth it.

questions.en: How has the way people use phones changed over the years? How is it different from when you were younger?
questions.ko: 사람들이 전화기를 사용하는 방식은 세월이 지나면서 어떻게 달라졌나요? 당신이 어렸을 때와 어떻게 다른가요?
tips: 과거(집 전화·문자·통화) → 현재(스마트폰·앱·SNS) → 장단점 → 내 생각
'Back in the day', 'These days, more and more people', 'used to' 패턴

answers.IM3: Phones have changed a lot. When I was a child, we had a home phone, and I called my friends on it. In middle school, I got my first cell phone. I used it only for calls and text messages. Now, I have a smartphone, and I use it for everything. I check the news, watch videos, pay for things, and take photos. I can't imagine living without my phone. It is very convenient, but I think I use it too much.
answers.IH: Wow, phones have changed more than almost anything else, I think. Back in the day, when I was in elementary school, we had one home phone in the living room, and I had to ask my mom before calling a friend. I got my first cell phone in middle school, and it was a small flip phone. I used it just for calls and texts, and I remember counting my text messages because they cost money. These days, more and more people use their phones for everything. I check the news, watch YouTube, pay at stores, order food, and even do my banking on my phone. To be honest, I probably touch my phone more than 100 times a day. The good thing is that it's incredibly convenient, but the downside is that it can be addictive. I sometimes catch myself scrolling for an hour without noticing. Compared to when I was younger, we're more connected but maybe a little less present. Still, I can't imagine going back.
answers.AL: Phones have probably changed more than any other part of daily life. When I was in elementary school, we had one landline in the living room, and calling a friend meant getting past their parents first. I got my first cell phone in middle school, a little flip phone, and it was strictly for calls and texts. I remember rationing my text messages because each one cost money, and typing a single sentence took forever on that number pad. Fast-forward to now, and my phone is basically my wallet, my newspaper, my TV, my map, and my bank, all rolled into one. I pay for coffee with it, order groceries with it, and even unlock my front door with it. These days, more and more people are glued to their screens, and I'm no exception. If I'm being honest, I probably pick up my phone well over a hundred times a day. The upside is that it's incredibly convenient. The downside is that it's hard to put down, and I've caught myself scrolling for an hour without meaning to. Compared to when I was a kid, we're far more connected, but I'm not sure we're more present. Looking back, I can't believe how much has changed in such a short time. Still, I wouldn't want to go back to that flip phone.

questions.en: What do you usually do on the internet? Tell me about the websites or apps you use most and when you use them.
questions.ko: 인터넷에서 보통 무엇을 하나요? 가장 많이 쓰는 웹사이트나 앱, 그리고 언제 사용하는지 말해 주세요.

answers.IM3: I use the internet every day, mostly on my phone. In the morning, I check the weather and the news. During the day, I use email and a messenger app for work. In the evening, I watch YouTube or Netflix for about an hour. I also shop online a lot because it's easy. On weekends, I look for restaurants and cafes on my phone. I probably spend three or four hours a day online. It is a big part of my life.
answers.IH: Well, I'm online pretty much all day, like most people my age. The first thing I do in the morning is check the weather and skim the news on my phone. During work, I'm mostly on email and our team messenger, and I use Google to look things up. On the subway home, I usually watch short videos or listen to a podcast. In the evening, I spend about an hour on YouTube or Netflix, and I often shop online for groceries or small things I need. Actually, I do most of my shopping online these days because delivery is so fast in Korea. On weekends, I use map apps and review apps to find new cafes and restaurants. I'd say I spend at least four hours a day online, not counting work. The thing is, it's so convenient that it's easy to lose track of time. I've started putting my phone away an hour before bed, and that's helped a lot.
answers.AL: I'm online more or less from the moment I wake up until I go to bed, which I suspect is true for most people my age. My morning starts with a quick scroll through the weather and headlines on my phone before I've even gotten out of bed. Once I'm at work, it's mostly email, our team messaging app, and a lot of Google searches, since my job involves researching new projects. The subway ride home is usually podcast time, or if I'm too tired to focus, I'll watch short videos. In the evening, I settle in with YouTube or Netflix for an hour or so, and I do a surprising amount of shopping from the sofa. Groceries, household stuff, even clothes: it all gets ordered online because delivery in Korea is ridiculously fast. On weekends, I lean heavily on map and review apps to hunt down new cafes and restaurants. If I had to guess, I'd say I'm online at least four or five hours a day outside of work. The thing is, it's all so convenient that it's easy to lose an entire evening without noticing. So lately, I've been trying to put my phone in another room an hour before bed. It's a small change, but I sleep noticeably better.

questions.en: Tell me about a memorable holiday you celebrated, like Chuseok or New Year's. What did you do, who were you with, and why was it special?
questions.ko: 추석이나 설날처럼 기억에 남는 명절에 대해 말해 주세요. 무엇을 했고, 누구와 함께였으며, 왜 특별했나요?
tips: 언제(몇 년 전 추석) → 어디로 갔나 → 무슨 일 → 특별했던 점 → 느낌, 과거시제
'Speaking of holidays, I remember ~' 로 자연스럽게 시작

answers.IM3: The Chuseok I remember most was three years ago. My family went to my grandmother's house in Daegu. The drive took six hours because of the traffic. We made songpyeon, which is a rice cake, together in the kitchen. My grandmother taught me how to make it. Mine looked a little ugly, but they tasted good. In the evening, we ate a big dinner and looked at the full moon. It was special because all my cousins were there. I felt very happy.
answers.IH: Speaking of holidays, the one I remember most is Chuseok three years ago. My whole family drove down to my grandmother's house in Daegu. The trip usually takes about four hours, but because of the holiday traffic, it took almost seven. We were all pretty grumpy when we arrived. But then my grandmother had us all sit in the kitchen and make songpyeon, the rice cakes we eat on Chuseok, together. She showed me how to shape them, and mine came out pretty ugly, which made everyone laugh. In the evening, we had a huge dinner with about fifteen people and went outside to look at the full moon. What made it special was that all seven of my cousins were there for the first time in years. We stayed up late playing card games and talking about old memories. To be honest, I hadn't felt that close to my family in a long time. My grandmother passed away last year, so that Chuseok means even more to me now.
answers.AL: Speaking of holidays, the one that always comes to mind is Chuseok from three years ago. My whole family piled into two cars and drove down to my grandmother's house in Daegu. The trip normally takes about four hours, but with holiday traffic, it dragged on for nearly seven, so by the time we pulled in, everyone was cranky. My grandmother, though, wasn't having any of that. She sat all of us down in the kitchen and had us make songpyeon together, which are the little rice cakes we eat on Chuseok. She'd been making them for sixty years, so hers were perfect, and mine looked like lumpy little rocks. My cousins teased me about it all night. That evening, about fifteen of us squeezed around the table for a huge dinner, and afterward we went out to the yard to look at the full moon. What made it so special was that all seven of my cousins were there at the same time, which hadn't happened since we were kids. We ended up staying up until two in the morning, playing card games and digging up old stories. It was one of those nights where you don't realize how much it means until later. My grandmother passed away last year, so that Chuseok has become one of my most precious memories.

questions.en: Tell me about your favorite piece of furniture in your home. What does it look like, where is it, and why do you like it?
questions.ko: 집에서 가장 좋아하는 가구에 대해 말해 주세요. 어떻게 생겼고, 어디에 있으며, 왜 좋아하나요?
tips: 무엇 → 위치 → 생김새(색·재질·크기) → 언제 샀는지 → 왜 좋은지(용도·추억)
'It's where I ~', 'I bought it when ~' 로 의미 부여

answers.IM3: My favorite piece of furniture is my sofa. It's in the living room, in front of the TV. It's a big gray sofa with soft cushions. I bought it two years ago when I moved into this apartment. I like it because it is very comfortable. After work, I lie on the sofa and watch TV. On weekends, I read books there with a cup of coffee. Sometimes I even fall asleep on it. It's the best spot in my home.
answers.IH: Hmm, that's an easy one. It's definitely my sofa. It's a big gray three-seater in the living room, right across from the TV, and it has these really soft cushions that you sink into. I bought it about two years ago when I moved into this apartment, and to be honest, it was more expensive than I planned. But I've never regretted it. It's where I spend most of my time at home. After work, I lie there and watch a drama, and on weekend mornings, I sit in the corner with a cup of coffee and read. Actually, I've fallen asleep on it more times than I can count. Before this, I used to have a cheap hard sofa that hurt my back, so the difference is huge. My friends always say it's the most comfortable sofa they've ever sat on. It's not just furniture to me; it's where I relax and recharge.
answers.AL: Oh, that's easy. It's my sofa, without a doubt. It's a big gray three-seater that sits in the living room, right across from the TV, and it's got these deep, soft cushions that you just sink into. I bought it about two years ago when I moved into this apartment, and I'll admit I went over budget on it. At the time, I felt a little guilty, but it's turned out to be the best purchase I've made for this place. It's basically where my life at home happens. After a long day, I'll collapse onto it and put on a drama, and on weekend mornings, I curl up in the corner seat with a coffee and a book while the sun comes through the balcony door. I've lost count of how many times I've dozed off on it and woken up at two in the morning. Before this, I had a cheap, stiff sofa that left my back aching, so the upgrade felt life-changing. Whenever friends come over, they end up fighting over the corner spot. What I love most is that it's not just a piece of furniture; it's where I unwind, recharge, and honestly, where I feel most at home.

questions.en: Have you ever had a problem at a bank or with a banking app? Tell me what happened and how you solved it.
questions.ko: 은행이나 은행 앱을 쓰다가 문제를 겪은 적이 있나요? 무슨 일이 있었고 어떻게 해결했는지 말해 주세요.
tips: 언제 → 무슨 문제(앱 오류·송금 실수·카드 분실) → 내가 한 행동 → 결과 → 배운 점
'It turned out that ~', 'I was so relieved when ~' 으로 결과와 감정 표현

answers.IM3: Yes, I had a problem last year. I sent money to a friend using my banking app. But I typed the wrong account number. The money went to a stranger. I was very worried. So I called the bank right away. The bank staff was kind and explained the process. It took about a week, but I got my money back. Now I always check the account number twice.
answers.IH: Yes, actually, I had a pretty stressful one last year. I was sending money to a friend through my banking app for a birthday gift we were buying together. I was in a hurry, and I typed one number wrong in the account number. The money, about 200,000 won, went to a complete stranger. When I realized it, my heart dropped. I called the bank's customer service right away, and to be honest, I was almost crying on the phone. The staff was really kind and told me that they would contact the other person's bank. It turned out that the person was honest and agreed to send it back. The whole process took about a week, and I was so relieved when the money finally came back. Since then, I always double-check the account number and the name before I press send. It was a small mistake, but it taught me to slow down, especially when money is involved.
answers.AL: Yes, and it still makes me cringe a little. Last year, a few friends and I were chipping in for a birthday gift, and I was sending my share to the friend who was organizing it. I was on the subway, in a rush, and I fat-fingered one digit of the account number. The app asked me to confirm, and I just tapped through without reading. Two hundred thousand won, gone to a complete stranger. The moment I saw the unfamiliar name in the confirmation, my stomach dropped. I got off at the next station and called the bank's customer service right there on the platform. The rep was incredibly patient and walked me through the process. Basically, they contacted the recipient's bank, which then asked the account holder to send the money back. It turned out the person was honest and returned it, but the whole thing took about a week, and I checked the app about ten times a day the entire time. When the money finally showed up, I was so relieved I actually laughed out loud. Looking back, it was a cheap lesson. Now I read the recipient's name twice before I hit send, no matter how much of a hurry I'm in.

pronunciation.tip: th는 혀를 이 사이에 살짝 넣고 성대 울리기. 'whether'와 발음 같음
첫 음절 강세. b 뒤에 모음 넣지 말기('서브웨이' 아니라 '섭웨이')
